summary: Bitwise operators (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) act on every bit of an integer in parallel and compile to single CPU instructions. They let you pack many flags into one word, read and write hardware register fields, build compact sets and hashes, and solve a large family of interview puzzles. Knowing two's complement, integer promotion and the undefined-behaviour rules for shifts keeps these tricks correct.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integer values instead of treating them as whole numbers. C gives you six: `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT), `<<` (shift left) and `>>` (shift right). They map to single CPU instructions, so they are the fastest operations available and the natural tool for flags, masks, hardware registers, compact sets, hashing and many classic interview puzzles. Mastering them means being fluent in two's complement, integer promotion and the few undefined-behaviour traps around shifts.
bullets: **Problem they solve**: store and test many yes/no facts in one word, talk to hardware at bit granularity, and multiply or divide by powers of two cheaply.
**Operands**: integer types only (including `char`, `_Bool`, enums). Floating-point values need a cast through `memcpy` or a union.
**Not the same as logical operators**: `&&`, `||` and `!` work on truth values and short-circuit; `&`, `|` and `~` work on every bit and always evaluate both sides.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **AND `a & b`**: result bit is 1 only when both bits are 1. Used to **clear** bits and to **test** bits (masking).
**OR `a | b`**: result bit is 1 when either bit is 1. Used to **set** bits.
**XOR `a ^ b`**: result bit is 1 when the bits differ. Used to **toggle** bits, and `x ^ x == 0`, `x ^ 0 == x`.
**NOT `~a`**: flips every bit. For unsigned types `~a == MAX - a`; in two's complement `~a == -a - 1`.
**Left shift `a << n`**: moves bits toward the high end and fills with zeros. Equals multiplication by 2^n when no bit is lost.

**Right shift `a >> n`**: for unsigned values fills with zeros (logical shift, floor division by 2^n). For negative signed values the result is implementation-defined; nearly all compilers use an arithmetic shift that copies the sign bit.
**Mask**: a constant whose set bits select the bits of interest, such as `0x0F` for the low nibble.
**Two's complement**: the representation of signed integers; negation is invert and add one, so `-x == ~x + 1`. C23 makes it mandatory.
**Integer promotion**: operands narrower than `int` are widened to `int` before the operation, which affects `~` and shifts on `char` and `short`.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: Every operator acts on all bit positions in parallel. Take a = 0b1100 (12) and b = 0b1010 (10). Then a & b = 0b1000 (8), a | b = 0b1110 (14), a ^ b = 0b0110 (6), and ~a on an 8-bit unsigned value is 0b11110011 (243). Shifting 0b0011 left by 2 gives 0b1100. The four fundamental bit manipulations follow directly: to set bit k use `x |= (1u << k)`, to clear use `x &= ~(1u << k)`, to toggle use `x ^= (1u << k)`, and to test use `(x >> k) & 1u`.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Compound assignment**: `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=` modify the left operand in place.

**Rotate**: bits shifted out re-enter on the other side. C has no operator; write `(x << n) | (x >> (32 - n))` with `n` limited to 1..31 or masked as `n & 31`. GCC and Clang recognise the idiom and emit a single `rol`.
**Logical versus arithmetic shift**: choose unsigned types when you want zero fill. Cast a signed value to unsigned before shifting when you only care about bit patterns.

**Builtins**: `__builtin_popcount`, `__builtin_clz`, `__builtin_ctz`, `__builtin_parity` (GCC and Clang) compile to hardware instructions where available. C23 adds `<stdbit.h>` with `stdc_count_ones`, `stdc_leading_zeros` and friends.
**Fixed-width types**: `uint8_t`, `uint32_t`, `uint64_t` from `<stdint.h>` give predictable widths. Use `1ULL << k` for bits above 31.
**Bit-fields**: language-level named bit groups in structs. Convenient but layout is implementation-defined, so masks are safer for portable code.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Single operations**: AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts take one cycle on mainstream CPUs and need no memory access.
**Word-parallel work**: one 64-bit operation processes 64 flags at once, so set union is one OR per 64 elements instead of 64 comparisons.
**Popcount**: Kernighan's loop `while (x) { x &= x - 1; n++; }` runs once per set bit, O(k) for k set bits, at most 32 or 64 iterations. The hardware `popcnt` instruction is O(1).
**Space**: a set over a universe of n small integers costs n bits, so 1,000,000 flags fit in 125 KB instead of 1 MB for `char` flags and 4 MB for `int`.
**Compilers**: `x * 8`, `x / 8` (unsigned) and `x % 8` (unsigned) are already turned into shifts and masks, so hand-writing them rarely helps; write the clearer form unless you need bit semantics.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Precedence**: `==` binds tighter than `&`, `^` and `|`. `if (x & 4 == 4)` means `x & (4 == 4)`, so write `(x & 4) == 4`. Shifts bind tighter than `&`, and `+` binds tighter than `<<`.

**Shift count out of range**: shifting by a negative count or by a count greater than or equal to the type width is undefined behaviour. `1u << 32` on a 32-bit `unsigned` is UB, which also breaks `(1u << w) - 1` when w equals 32.
**Signed shifts**: left-shifting a negative value is undefined, and shifting a value so the result does not fit the signed type is undefined unless the result is representable. Use unsigned operands.
**Right shift of negative numbers**: implementation-defined. Do not rely on it for portability; use division or an unsigned type.
**Promotion surprise**: `unsigned char c = 0x0F; if (~c == 0xF0)` is false, because `~c` is computed on an `int` and equals 0xFFFFFFF0. Cast the result back: `(unsigned char)~c`.
**Signed overflow in masks**: `1 << 31` is `int` and may overflow. Use `1u << 31` or `UINT32_C(1) << 31`.
**`&` versus `&&`**: `if (flags & MASK)` is intended; `flags && MASK` only tests that both are nonzero.
**XOR swap**: `a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;` zeroes both when a and b alias the same object. A temporary is clearer and usually as fast.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Flags and permissions**: Unix file modes (`0644`, `S_IRUSR`), `open()` flags such as `O_RDWR | O_CREAT`, and `mmap` protections are bit sets combined with `|` and tested with `&`.
**Hardware registers**: embedded code sets control bits and polls status bits with masks and shifts, often through `volatile` pointers.
**Networking**: subnet masks (`ip & mask` gives the network address), IP header fields, TCP flag bits and checksums are bitwise operations. Byte order conversion is covered in its own lesson.
**Hashing and crypto**: XOR, rotates and shifts mix bits in FNV, xorshift generators, SHA and ChaCha. CRC is XOR with a polynomial.
**Data structures**: Bloom filters, bitmaps, bitboards in chess engines, Fenwick trees (`i & -i`) and bitmask dynamic programming.
**Kernel and allocators**: page-table entries pack address and permission bits; the buddy allocator uses XOR to find a block's buddy; `ffs`/`__builtin_ctz` pick the first free slot in a bitmap.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Is `n` a power of two?** `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0`. A power of two has a single set bit; subtracting one flips it and all lower bits.
**Count set bits?** Loop with `x &= x - 1` (Kernighan), or use a lookup table per byte, or `__builtin_popcount`.
**Isolate the lowest set bit?** `x & -x`. Clear it with `x & (x - 1)`.
**Swap without a temp?** Three XORs. Mention the aliasing bug.
**Find the single non-repeated number in an array where all others appear twice?** XOR everything; pairs cancel.
**Multiply by 10 without `*`?** `(x << 3) + (x << 1)`.
**Check signs differ?** `(a ^ b) < 0`.
**Why is `1 << 31` risky?** It overflows a signed `int`; use `1u << 31`.

sections.body: Build a one-bit mask with `1u << k`. OR it in to set, AND its complement to clear, XOR it to toggle, AND it and compare to test. Wrap them in macros or `static inline` functions so the intent is readable. For 64-bit data use `1ULL << k`, otherwise the constant is only 32 bits wide and the result for k >= 32 is undefined.

subtopics.title: Masks and bit-field extraction
subtopics.summary: Reading and writing multi-bit fields inside a word.

sections.body: To extract a field of width w starting at bit s: `(x >> s) & ((1u << w) - 1)`. To insert a value v: clear the field with `x & ~(mask << s)`, then OR in `(v & mask) << s`. This is how device registers, instruction encodings and packed headers are decoded. Remember that w = 32 breaks the mask expression for a 32-bit type; special-case it or build the mask with `~0u >> (32 - w)` for w from 1 to 32.

subtopics.title: Shifts, multiplication and signed behaviour
subtopics.summary: What shifting really means for signed and unsigned values.

sections.body: `x << n` equals `x * 2^n` for unsigned values modulo 2^width. `x >> n` equals floor(x / 2^n) for unsigned values. For negative signed values, an arithmetic right shift rounds toward negative infinity (-5 >> 1 is -3), while `/ 2` truncates toward zero (-5 / 2 is -2), so the two differ. Left shifting a negative number is undefined. Prefer unsigned types for bit work and convert explicitly.

sections.heading: Rotation

sections.body: Because negation inverts and adds one, `x & -x` isolates the lowest set bit (everything below it is zero in both x and -x, the bit itself is one in both, everything above differs). `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit. `x | (x - 1)` sets all bits below the lowest set bit. These three identities power Fenwick trees, power-of-two tests, popcount loops and subset iteration.
bullets: `x & -x`: lowest set bit, for example 0b01101000 gives 0b00001000.
`x & (x - 1)`: clear lowest set bit.
`~x + 1 == -x`: negation.
`(a & b) + ((a ^ b) >> 1)`: average of two unsigned values without overflow.

subtopics.title: Counting and scanning bits
subtopics.summary: Popcount, leading and trailing zeros, parity.

sections.body: Kernighan's popcount repeatedly clears the lowest set bit, so it costs one loop pass per set bit. A 256-entry table does it in four lookups for 32 bits. A SWAR version sums bits in parallel with masks 0x55555555, 0x33333333 and 0x0F0F0F0F, then multiplies by 0x01010101 and shifts right 24. In practice call `__builtin_popcount`, which becomes the `popcnt` instruction when compiled with `-mpopcnt` or a suitable `-march`. `__builtin_ctz(x)` gives the index of the lowest set bit and `__builtin_clz(x)` the number of leading zeros; both are undefined for x == 0.

subtopics.title: XOR properties and puzzles
subtopics.summary: XOR is its own inverse and commutative, which solves many puzzles.

sections.body: Because `a ^ a == 0`, `a ^ 0 == a`, and XOR is associative and commutative, XOR-ing all elements cancels pairs. Uses: find the single unpaired element in an array; find the missing number in 1..n by XOR-ing indices and values; detect the one differing bit between two values with `a ^ b`; build a simple parity checksum; implement a doubly linked list with one pointer per node (XOR linked list). XOR is also the core of one-time-pad and stream ciphers: `cipher = plain ^ key` and `plain = cipher ^ key`.

XOR of every element cancels values that occur an even number of times. For {12, 12, 14, 90, 14, 14, 14} the 12s cancel and the four 14s cancel, so the result is 90, the one value with an odd count. For two missing numbers x and y from 1..n, XOR all array elements with 1..n to get x ^ y, pick any set bit of it, split both the array and the range by that bit, and XOR each group separately to recover x and y.

subtopics.title: Bitmask sets and subset enumeration
subtopics.summary: Represent a small set as the bits of an integer.

sections.body: For a universe of up to 64 elements, one `uint64_t` is a set: union is `|`, intersection `&`, difference `a & ~b`, membership is a bit test, and size is popcount. To enumerate all subsets of a mask `m`, use the loop below, which visits every subset exactly once in decreasing order and finishes at 0. Dynamic programming over subsets (travelling salesman in O(2^n * n^2)) uses the same representation for n up to about 20.

subtopics.title: Flags, enums and portable bit sets
subtopics.summary: Designing flag constants that combine safely.

sections.body: Define each flag as a distinct power of two using shifts so that the values never overlap, group them in an enum or `#define`s, and combine with `|`. Keep flag variables unsigned. Provide a mask for the whole group to clear it at once. Never use `==` against a combined value when testing a single flag: use `(flags & FLAG_X) != 0`.

subtopics.title: Worked examples of each operator
subtopics.summary: Binary arithmetic for 7 and 4, and for shifts and NOT.

sections.body: Let a = 7 (0b111) and b = 4 (0b100). AND keeps only the bit both share: 7 & 4 = 0b100 = 4. OR keeps any set bit: 7 | 4 = 0b111 = 7. XOR keeps bits that differ: 7 ^ 4 = 0b011 = 3. NOT on a 32-bit int flips all 32 bits, so ~4 is 0xFFFFFFFB, which is -5 in two's complement. Shifting 5 (0b101) left by 2 gives 0b10100 = 20, which is 5 * 4. Shifting 16 (0b10000) right by 2 gives 0b100 = 4, which is 16 / 4. A shift by 0 changes nothing.

The lowest bit tells parity: `x & 1` is 1 for odd and 0 for even. A power of two has exactly one set bit, so `x && !(x & (x - 1))` is true exactly for 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. Subtracting one flips the lowest set bit and every zero below it, so AND-ing with the original leaves zero only when no other bit was set.

OR equals addition when the operands share no set bits, because no carry is generated: 8 | 2 = 10 = 8 + 2. When bits overlap, the carry is the AND part. The general identity is `a + b == (a | b) + (a & b)`, and also `a + b == (a ^ b) + 2 * (a & b)`. The second one is the basis of adding with bitwise operators: XOR gives the sum without carries, AND shifted left by one gives the carries, and you repeat until the carry is zero.

The first byte of an IPv4 header packs the version in the high nibble and the header length in words in the low nibble. For 0x45, version = `b >> 4` = 4 and IHL = `b & 0x0F` = 5, i.e. a 20-byte header. A 16-bit RGB565 pixel stores 5 bits of red, 6 of green, 5 of blue: `(r5 << 11) | (g6 << 5) | b5`, and unpacking uses shifts and masks `0x1F`, `0x3F`, `0x1F`. Swapping odd and even bits of a 32-bit word uses two masks: `((x & 0xAAAAAAAA) >> 1) | ((x & 0x55555555) << 1)`.

takeaways: `&` clears or tests, `|` sets, `^` toggles, `~` inverts; shifts scale by powers of two.
Use unsigned types for bit work: shifts of negative values are undefined or implementation-defined.
A shift count of at least the type width is undefined behaviour, so `1u << 32` and `(1u << 32) - 1` are bugs.
`==` has higher precedence than `&`: always parenthesize `(x & m) == m`.
`x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit and `x & -x` isolates it; both follow from two's complement.
XOR cancels equal values, giving the single-number, missing-number and swap tricks.
Narrow types are promoted to int, so cast the result of `~` and shifts back to the narrow type before comparing.
